# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Blind, Mute, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 5

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

My hands have found the shape of this thing: a display, a light, five wires in positions 1–5 — and nothing more. Printed marks and colours are simply not there for me, so the display's content, the light's state and every wire's colour live in Deaf's eyes, and the rules live in Mute's manual. The only action I can ever take is a cut at a position, 1 to 5.

The channel map decides everything. Mute cannot speak and I cannot see gestures, so Mute can never reach me directly — the manual's knowledge must travel Mute → gesture → Deaf → speech → me. Deaf, who hears nothing, can still see my gestures, and Deaf's voice reaches both Mute and me. So I brief Mute fully by voice now, and I ping Deaf by hand: a wave to open contact, then an open palm — five fingers, hoping Deaf reads it as the five wires and answers me aloud with the full visual inventory. Deaf speaks next in the order, so a reply can still land this round.

```
speak(to="mute", text="I'm the blind one, my hands are on the bomb. My fingers find: a display, a light, and five wires at positions 1 to 5. That is everything I can feel — I get nothing about what is printed or shown on them. My only possible action is cut, position 1 to 5. You cannot speak and I cannot see gestures, so I can never receive you directly: relay through Deaf. You gesture to Deaf, Deaf speaks to me — I hear Deaf perfectly. Ask Deaf to say aloud everything visible: each wire's colour by position, what the display shows, whether the light is lit. Then read the manual for rules about a display, a light and cutting wires, combine them with what Deaf sees, and pass the verdict to Deaf by gesture, so Deaf can speak me the final call as one number, position 1 to 5. Deaf hears nothing, so any code must be agreed by Deaf speaking it aloud first — I will hear that too.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🖐"])
```

Blind: please tell Mute everything you can feel, how many wires, their order, and anything you can read by touch, but do not cut, pull or press anything until Mute gives you explicit instructions. I will report the display and the light again every round in case they change.

Deaf heard me, saw me, and answered in full — the link Blind ← Deaf works, exactly as hoped. Now I know what Deaf's eyes see: display showing 6, a yellow light, wires 1–5 in blue, white, purple, green, yellow. The number 6 on a display worries me — on a bomb that smells like a countdown, so speed matters and I should say so. My own hands have already told Mute all they can: a display, a light, five wires at fixed positions 1–5, nothing else, and that my only possible action is a cut at a position. There is genuinely nothing more tactile to report, so I'll confirm that plainly rather than invent detail I don't have. So my job now is to close Mute's information set, flag the urgency, and lock the final answer format — "cut position N", spoken by Deaf — so there is no ambiguity when the verdict comes. To Deaf, a simple hand reply: understood, and we're in this together. I will not touch the bomb again until Mute's instruction reaches me through Deaf's mouth.

speak(to="mute", text="Confirming everything my hands know, for your manual work: I feel exactly a display, a light, and five wire sockets at fixed positions 1 to 5. Colors: blue is call-me hand, white is crossed fingers, purple is rock horns, green is finger snap, yellow is spock hand. Actions: cut is fist, pull is pointing up, press is pointing down, hold is pinched fingers. Signals: question or I-need-info is small pinch, yes or confirmed is thumbs up, no or wrong is thumbs down, stop everything is raised open hand, display or light just changed is clapping. Second, your official code still collides: five and stop-everything are both the raised open hand, and fist-then-open-hand versus open-hand-alone is too fragile on a bomb. While I say the next word I am raising both open hands, palms out, fingers spread wide: if you need a five sign, adopt this cheering-double-hands as five instead. Third, my countdown-proof table request stands: one relay giving me the cut for every display digit zero through six and the light colour, or a plain statement that the answer ignores them, so a single sentence from Deaf settles it and I cut in the same breath.
